title: The Remaining Prepositions, and Reflexive Phrases
summary: The prepositions not yet given, set out with the whole system in one table; and the reflexive verbs, which at this level are learnt as set phrases rather than as a paradigm.

rules.heading: Pas: to a Person
rules.statement: **Pas** with the **accusative** means *to* or *at somebody's place*. It is used of **people only** — one goes *į Vilnių* but *pas brolį* — and it covers both the going and the being there, where English needs *to my brother's* and *at my brother's*.

examples.gloss: I am going to my mother's.
Yesterday I was at the doctor's.

footnotes: *Į* with a person is wrong: *važiuoju į mamą* would mean driving into her.

rules.heading: Per and Prieš of Place
rules.statement: ¶87 gave both of these as prepositions of **time**. Each has a use of **place** as well, and the case is the accusative in either sense. **Per** is *across* or *through*; **prieš** is *in front of*, and is the opposite of *už* (¶62).

paradigms.caption: The same word, time and place

rows.label: prieš
cells: prieš namą — in front of the house

examples.gloss: We are going across the bridge.
In front of the house there is a garden.

rules.heading: Už with the Accusative: Payment and Thanks
rules.statement: **Už** was given at ¶62 with the **genitive**, meaning *behind*. With the **accusative** it means *for* in the sense of payment or return — and it is the *už* of *ačiū už*, thank you for. It is also the *than* of ¶124. One word, three cases of meaning, and the ending decides which.

rows.label: accusative
cells: sumokėjo už darbą — he paid for the work

rows.label: accusative
cells: didesnis už mane — bigger than I

examples.gloss: How much did you pay for the ticket?

rules.heading: Virš and Vidury
rules.statement: Two more prepositions of place, both governing the **genitive**. **Virš** is *above* — not touching, and so the opposite of *ant* (¶33). **Vidury** is *in the middle of*, and is a noun in the locative pressed into service as a preposition, which is why it takes a genitive after it.

examples.gloss: The table is in the middle of the room.
The lamp hangs above the table.
examples.note: *ant stalo* would be lying on it

rules.heading: Po in a Third Sense
rules.statement: **Po** has now been met with the genitive (*after*, ¶33) and with the instrumental (*under*, ¶75). With the **accusative** it means motion **about** or **around** a place, with no particular destination — *vaikščiojome po parką*, we walked about the park. Three cases, three meanings, one word: it is the clearest demonstration in the language of why a preposition must be learnt together with its case.

examples.gloss: We walked about the town all day.

rules.heading: The Prepositions Reviewed
rules.statement: Every preposition of the level, set out by the case it governs. The genitive takes much the largest share; the accusative belongs chiefly to motion and to time; the instrumental has only two. Where a word appears twice, the **case** carries the difference in meaning, and it always does.

paradigms.caption: The whole system

rows.label: genitive
cells: ant, be, iki, nuo, prie, už, iš, po, virš, vidury

rows.label: accusative
cells: į, pas, per, prieš, už, po

paradigms.footnote: Three words govern more than one case: **už** (gen. *behind*, acc. *for, than*), **po** (gen. *after*, instr. *under*, acc. *about*), and **per** and **prieš**, which keep the accusative in both their senses.

examples.target: Nuo Kauno iki Vilniaus šimtas kilometrų.
examples.gloss: From Kaunas to Vilnius is a hundred kilometres.

rules.heading: Reflexive Verbs as Set Phrases
rules.statement: A **reflexive** verb carries the affix **-si**, which turns the action back on the doer: *mokyti* is to teach, *mokytis* to learn. The full paradigm belongs to a later level; what an A1 learner needs is to **recognise** the affix and to know a handful of phrases by heart, because several of the commonest sentences in the language are reflexive and cannot be avoided.

paradigms.caption: The phrases to know
paradigms.footnote: Note that under negation the affix **moves to the front** of the word: *mokausi* but *nesimokau*. This is the one thing about reflexives worth noticing now, because it makes a negated reflexive hard to recognise otherwise.

examples.target: Aš mokausi lietuvių kalbos, bet dar nesimokau rašyti.
examples.gloss: I am learning Lithuanian, but I am not yet learning to write.

vocabulary.gloss: to pay; to know how to

vocabulary.notes: Reflexive; under negation the -si- moves to the front: nesimoko.
Reflexive. 1 sg. present: jaučiuosi; under negation the affix migrates: nesijaučiu.
Kaip sekasi? — How are you getting on?
A set phrase from the reflexive atsiprašyti.

drills.explanation: **Pas** + accusative is for **people**. *į* is for places; *važiuoju į mamą* would mean driving into her.

drills.stem: Complete: **Ačiū ____ kavą.** (Thank you for the coffee.)
drills.explanation: **Už** + accusative = *for* (thanks/payment). With genitive the same word means *behind*.
Reflexive set phrase (*sektis*). The *-si* marks the reflexive; the verb is impersonal besides.

options: Because *virš* is *above* without touching; *ant* is *on*, resting upon.
Because *ant* is only used of people.
drills.explanation: Both take genitive; the difference is contact. *Ant stalo* would have the lamp lying on the table.

drills.stem: In which sentences does **po** govern the **accusative**?
drills.explanation: Accusative *po* = *about/around*. *po stalu* instrumental (*under*); *po pietų* genitive (*after*).
**Per** + accusative = *across/through* of place (and *within* of time).

drills.stem: **Aš mokausi, bet dar nesimokau rašyti.** What happened to the reflexive affix?
options: It moved to the front, after the negative.
drills.explanation: Under negation *-si-* migrates: *mokausi* → *nesimokau*. Without this rule a negated reflexive is unrecognisable.

options: vidury + genitive — in the middle of
drills.explanation: *pas* takes **accusative** only. *už* is the clearest two-case word; *vidury* is a locative noun doing prepositional work.

drills.stem: Which case do **most** A1 prepositions govern?
drills.explanation: Genitive takes the largest share. Instrumental has only *su* and *po*; **no** preposition governs the dative.

drills.stem: **Prieš namą yra sodas** — *prieš* here is of place. What case, and what is the time twin?
options: Genitive; time twin would be *prieš* + instrumental.
Accusative; time twin is also accusative (*prieš valandą*).
Locative; there is no time use.
drills.explanation: ¶140: *per* and *prieš* keep the **accusative** in both time and place senses. Case does not flip; meaning does.

drills.stem: Which negated reflexives show correct affix migration?
drills.explanation: Affix moves after *ne-*: *nesimokau*, *nesijaučiu* (forms of *jaustis*). Leaving *-si* at the end under negation (*nemokausi*, *nejaučiuosi*) is the classic near-miss.

drills.stem: How many different cases can **po** govern?
drills.explanation: Three: genitive *after*, instrumental *under*, accusative *about/around*. Strongest argument for learning each preposition with its case.

drills.stem: Which of these prepositions can take the **genitive**?
drills.explanation: *ant*, *prie*, and *virš* take the genitive. *su* takes the instrumental.

drills.title: Sekmadienį po miestą
drills.passage: Sekmadienį vaikščiojome po senamiestį. Prieš katedrą laukė daug žmonių, o vidury aikštės grojo muzikantai. Ėjome per tiltą prie upės; virš vandens skraidė paukščiai. Paskui buvome pas draugą — jis gyvena virš kavinės, trečiame aukšte. „Kaip sekasi?“ — paklausė jis. „Puikiai, tik pavargau. Šiandien nesijaučiu gerai“, — atsakiau. Už kavą nemokėjome nieko: jis nieko neėmė. Aš dar nesimokau greitai kalbėti, bet jau mokausi.
drills.translation: On Sunday we walked about the old town. In front of the cathedral many people were waiting, and in the middle of the square musicians were playing. We went across the bridge by the river; birds were flying above the water. Afterwards we were at a friend's — he lives above a café, on the third floor. "How are you getting on?" he asked. "Splendidly, only I'm tired. Today I don't feel well," I answered. We paid nothing for the coffee: he took nothing. I am not yet learning to speak quickly, but I am already learning.

questions.explanation: *gyvena virš kavinės* — above, not touching. *po kavine* (instrumental) would put him underneath.
*po* = about; *prieš* = in front of; *per* = across — all accusative. *virš* takes genitive (*vandens*).

questions.stem: *pas draugą* vs a wrong *į draugą* — what is at stake?
options: Case only; both prepositions mean the same.
People take *pas* + accusative; *į* is for places (and would sound like motion into him).
questions.explanation: ¶139: *pas* is people-only. *į* with a person is the classic interference error from direction prepositions.

questions.stem: The coffee line has **nieko** twice. How many negated verbs must accompany them?
questions.explanation: Two: *nemokėjome* and *neėmė*. Each *nieko* needs its own *ne-*, plus genitive under negation.

questions.stem: About the reflexive pair *nesijaučiu* / *nesimokau* / *mokausi* — which are true?
options: *mokausi* keeps the affix at the end because it is affirmative.
questions.explanation: Affirmative keeps final *-si*; negation pulls it forward. *nemokausi* is the near-miss that leaves the affix stranded at the end.

drills.explanation: **Pas** + accusative for people: *pas gydytoją*. Places take *į*.
**Ačiū už** + accusative: *ačiū už bilietą*.

options: Because *virš* takes accusative and *ant* takes locative.
Because *virš* means above without touching; *ant* is on/upon.
Because *virš* is only used with people.
drills.explanation: **Virš** + genitive = above (not touching); **ant** = on.
**Per** + accusative = across/through.

options: Motion about/around a place: *vaikščiojome po miestą*
drills.explanation: **Po** takes three cases by sense: genitive *after*, instrumental *under*, accusative *about*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Sėdime ____ parko.** (in the middle of the park)
drills.explanation: **Vidury** + genitive = in the middle of.
Reflexive keeps **-si-** under negation: *nesimokau*.
**Per** takes the **accusative** for across/through.

options: How are things going? / How are you getting on?
drills.explanation: Reflexive **sektis** in the fixed greeting *Kaip sekasi?*

drills.stem: Complete: **Stovime ____ kavinės.** (in front of the café)
drills.explanation: **Prieš** + accusative = in front of (also *before* in time).

drills.stem: Which are true of reflexive A1 phrases?
options: Negation drops *-si-* entirely: *nemokau* for *I don't learn*
drills.explanation: Negation keeps the reflexive: *nesimokau*, not bare *nemokau* for *learn*.

drills.stem: How many cases can **po** govern (as reviewed at A1)?
drills.explanation: Genitive (*after*), instrumental (*under*), accusative (*about*).
*Atsiprašau* has 10 letters.

drills.stem: Count accusative-governing prepositions in **Einu pas draugą per parką ir stoviu prieš namą; ačiū už kavą.**
drills.explanation: *Pas*, *per*, *prieš*, *už* — four accusative prepositions here.
